l: Pylos, The Iliad, And now, O Muses, dwellers in the mansions of Olympus, tell
s: Pylos sends a contingent from Pylos, Arene, and neighboring places. These forces bring ninety ships and are commanded by Nestor.

l: Nestor, The Iliad, And now, O Muses, dwellers in the mansions of Olympus, tell
s: Nestor commands the men of Pylos and the surrounding territories, who bring ninety ships. He is the only man said to rival Menestheus in arranging chariots and foot soldiers because he is older.

l: Ithaca, The Iliad, And now, O Muses, dwellers in the mansions of Olympus, tell
s: Ithaca is held by the Cephallenians, who also occupy Neritum, Crocylea, Aegilips, Samos, Zacynthus, and nearby mainland. These people bring twelve ships under Ulysses.

l: Ulysses, The Iliad, And now, O Muses, dwellers in the mansions of Olympus, tell
s: Ulysses leads the Cephallenians from Ithaca and the neighboring islands and mainland. He brings twelve ships and is praised as the equal of Jove in counsel.

l: Achilles, The Iliad, And now, O Muses, dwellers in the mansions of Olympus, tell
s: Achilles commands fifty ships from Phthia, Hellas, and neighboring lands, but his people take no part in the fighting because he remains by the ships. He is described as greater than Ajax son of Telamon and as having better horses, and he is expected to rejoin the battle before long.

l: Trojans, The Iliad, And now, O Muses, dwellers in the mansions of Olympus, tell
s: The Trojans gather with their allies outside the city after Iris warns them of the approaching host. Hector commands them, while the allied contingents include the Dardanians, Phrygians, Carians, Lycians, and many other peoples.

l: Iris, The Iliad, And now, O Muses, dwellers in the mansions of Olympus, tell
s: Iris is sent by Jove to bring the Trojans bad news about the advancing Achaeans. Disguised with the voice and likeness of Polites, she urges Hector to have each allied chief organize and lead his own people.

l: Priam, The Iliad, And now, O Muses, dwellers in the mansions of Olympus, tell
s: Priam is present at the assembly of old and young Trojans at the city gates. Iris addresses him as an old man and tells him that he speaks idly while the advancing host approaches.

l: Troy, The Iliad, And now, O Muses, dwellers in the mansions of Olympus, tell
s: Troy is represented by the city of Priam, before which the Trojans and their allies divide their forces. A high mound called Batieia stands before the city and serves as the place where the forces form up.

l: Hector, The Iliad, And now, O Muses, dwellers in the mansions of Olympus, tell
s: Hector recognizes that Iris is a goddess and immediately breaks up the assembly. He organizes the city’s defense and commands the Trojans, who comprise the greater number and most valiant of the forces eager for battle.

l: Aeneas, The Iliad, And now, O Muses, dwellers in the mansions of Olympus, tell
s: Aeneas leads the Dardanians. He is the son of Anchises and Venus, and he commands alongside Antenor’s sons Archelochus and Acamas.

l: Sarpedon, The Iliad, And now, O Muses, dwellers in the mansions of Olympus, tell
s: Sarpedon leads the Lycians together with Glaucus. Their forces come from their distant land beside the waters of the Xanthus.

l: Glaucus, The Iliad, And now, O Muses, dwellers in the mansions of Olympus, tell
s: Glaucus leads the Lycians together with Sarpedon. The Lycian contingent comes from the distant land by the eddying waters of the Xanthus.

l: ships of the Achaeans, The Iliad, And now, O Muses, dwellers in the mansions of Olympus, tell
s: The unit counts the ships supplied by the various Danaan contingents, ranging from two ships brought by Guneus to a hundred under Agamemnon. The ships are used to transport and station the forces, while Achilles’s ships remain apart from the fighting.

l: the Trojan War, The Iliad, And now, O Muses, dwellers in the mansions of Olympus, tell
s: The Trojan War is presented through the mustering of the Danaan and Trojan forces for battle. The unit focuses on the commanders, allies, ships, and formations preparing for renewed fighting.

l: Achaeans’ advance, The Iliad, And now, O Muses, dwellers in the mansions of Olympus, tell
s: The Achaeans’ advance is so vast that Iris compares them to leaves or the sands of the sea. Their movement across the plain makes the earth groan, and their approach prompts the Trojans to arm and organize.

l: Achilles’ anger, The Iliad, And now, O Muses, dwellers in the mansions of Olympus, tell
s: Achilles’ anger at Agamemnon keeps him and his people from taking part in the battle. While he remains by the ships, his men spend their time on the seashore instead of fighting.

l: Briseis’s loss, The Iliad, And now, O Muses, dwellers in the mansions of Olympus, tell
s: Briseis’s loss is the cause of Achilles’ continuing grief and withdrawal from the fighting. She had been taken by Achilles after the sack of Lyrnessus and Thebe, but Agamemnon’s quarrel with him leaves her loss at the center of his anger.

l: The Iliad, The Iliad, BOOK III.
s: Alexandrus challenges the Achaeans, but he retreats when Menelaus confronts him, prompting Hector to rebuke him and Alexandrus to propose single combat for Helen and her wealth. The Trojans and Achaeans agree to a covenant of peace if either champion wins, and Priam comes to witness the oath before returning to Troy. Menelaus overpowers Alexandrus in the duel, but Venus rescues Alexandrus and carries him to his bedchamber. Helen reproaches Alexandrus for his defeat, while Venus compels her to join him.

l: Alexandrus, The Iliad, BOOK III.
s: Alexandrus comes forward as the Trojan champion but retreats in fear when he sees Menelaus. After Hector rebukes him, he proposes that he and Menelaus fight for Helen and her wealth. He is defeated by Menelaus, rescued by Venus, and later urges Helen to join him.

l: Menelaus, The Iliad, BOOK III.
s: Menelaus eagerly faces Alexandrus, seeking revenge for the wrong done to him. In single combat he pierces Alexandrus's shield and cuirass, breaks his sword against Alexandrus's helmet, and drags him by the helmet plume until Venus intervenes.

l: Helen, The Iliad, BOOK III.
s: Helen is summoned to view the warriors and mourns her former husband, city, parents, and former life. From the tower she identifies Agamemnon, Ulysses, Ajax, and Idomeneus for Priam, while lamenting that Castor and Pollux are absent. After Alexandrus's defeat, she reproaches him and resists Venus before being forced to follow her to Alexandrus.

l: Hector, The Iliad, BOOK III.
s: Hector harshly rebukes Alexandrus for lacking courage and bringing ruin upon Troy. He announces Alexandrus's proposal for single combat, restrains the Trojan ranks, and later measures the ground and casts lots with Ulysses to determine who will fight first.

l: Priam, The Iliad, BOOK III.
s: Priam agrees to come to the plain and swear to the covenant. He asks Helen to identify the leading Achaean warriors, then returns to Troy before the combat because he cannot bear to watch his son fight.

l: Agamemnon, The Iliad, BOOK III.
s: Agamemnon orders the Achaeans to stop shooting so Hector can speak and tells Talthybius to bring the Achaean sacrificial lamb. He leads the oath ceremony, prays to Jove and other powers, and declares the terms for returning Helen and imposing a fine.

l: Venus, The Iliad, BOOK III.
s: Venus breaks the strap of Alexandrus's helmet and then hides him in a cloud of darkness, carrying him to his bedchamber. Disguised as an old woman, she summons Helen and threatens her until Helen follows her to Alexandrus.

l: Jove, The Iliad, BOOK III.
s: Jove is invoked as witness and guardian of the covenant, and the Trojans and Achaeans pray that oath-breakers and their children be punished. Menelaus and both armies also pray to Jove for victory over the one who began the war, but Jove does not yet grant their prayer.

l: Troy, The Iliad, BOOK III.
s: Troy is threatened by the conflict Alexandrus has brought upon the city, its people, and its children. Priam returns through the Scaean gates to Troy before the duel begins.

l: Achaeans, The Iliad, BOOK III.
s: The Achaeans advance silently and stand ready to fight the Trojans. They accept the proposed single combat and covenant, participate in the oath ceremony, and pray that the war's instigator will die so that they may return home in peace.

l: Trojans, The Iliad, BOOK III.
s: The Trojans advance noisily, then agree to let Alexandrus fight Menelaus for Helen and her wealth. They help prepare the oath offerings, pray for the punishment of oath-breakers, and remain subject to the danger Alexandrus has brought upon them.

l: battle, The Iliad, BOOK III.
s: The war is presented as having arisen from Alexandrus carrying Helen away from her husband and homeland. Both sides briefly hope that the single combat will settle the dispute and allow the armies to separate.

l: single combat between Paris and Menelaus, The Iliad, BOOK III.
s: The combat is arranged as a contest for Helen and her wealth, with the victor taking her and the defeated side accepting peace. Menelaus gains the advantage after Alexandrus's spear fails, piercing Alexandrus's defenses and dragging him away before Venus rescues him.

l: the covenant of peace, The Iliad, BOOK III.
s: The covenant requires the Trojans and Achaeans to lay down their arms and accept the victor's claim to Helen and her wealth. Priam, Agamemnon, and the assembled leaders swear that the Achaeans will return home and the Trojans will remain in Troy, but the covenant is not fulfilled because Venus removes Alexandrus from the fight.

l: Paris's defeat, The Iliad, BOOK III.
s: Paris's spear fails to pierce Menelaus's shield, while Menelaus's spear passes through Paris's shield and cuirass. Menelaus then breaks his sword against Paris's helmet and captures him by the helmet plume before Venus intervenes.

l: Paris's rescue by Venus, The Iliad, BOOK III.
s: Venus saves Paris by breaking the helmet strap, hiding him in darkness, and carrying him to his bedchamber. She then brings Helen to him despite Helen's anger and refusal.

l: The Iliad, The Iliad, Thus they laid themselves on the bed together; but the son of
s: Alexandrus could not be found among the Trojans or their allies, who hated him. Agamemnon announced that the victory had been with Menelaus. He called for Helen and her wealth to be returned and for a fine to be paid as a lasting testimony. The Achaeans shouted in applause.

l: Agamemnon, The Iliad, Thus they laid themselves on the bed together; but the son of
s: Agamemnon, king of men, announced that the victory had been with Menelaus. He demanded that Helen and her wealth be returned and that a fine be paid as agreed.

l: Menelaus, The Iliad, Thus they laid themselves on the bed together; but the son of
s: Menelaus was declared to have won the victory.

l: Alexandrus, The Iliad, Thus they laid themselves on the bed together; but the son of
s: Alexandrus could not be found among the Trojans or their allies. They hated him and had no intention of hiding him if they had seen him.

l: Helen, The Iliad, Thus they laid themselves on the bed together; but the son of
s: Agamemnon demanded that Helen be given back with all her wealth.

l: Trojans, The Iliad, Thus they laid themselves on the bed together; but the son of
s: The Trojans could not find Alexandrus. They hated him and would not have hidden him if they had seen him.

l: Danaans, The Iliad, Thus they laid themselves on the bed together; but the son of
s: The Achaeans shouted in applause after Agamemnon spoke.

l: victory, The Iliad, Thus they laid themselves on the bed together; but the son of
s: The victory was declared to have been with Menelaus.

l: fine, The Iliad, Thus they laid themselves on the bed together; but the son of
s: Agamemnon called for a fine to be paid as agreed, as a testimony among those born thereafter.

l: The Iliad, The Iliad, BOOK IV.
s: Jove, Juno, and Minerva quarrel on Olympus over whether the conflict between the Trojans and Achaeans should end in peace or continue in war. At Jove’s command, Minerva persuades Pandarus to violate the oaths by shooting Menelaus with an arrow, but the gods protect Menelaus and the wound is not mortal. Agamemnon summons Machaon, who removes the arrow and treats Menelaus’s wound. The attack renews hostility between the two sides and prepares them to resume fighting.

l: Jove, The Iliad, BOOK IV.
s: Jove counsels with the gods on Olympus and suggests either renewing the fighting or making peace between the Trojans and Achaeans. He becomes angry with Juno but ultimately orders Minerva to make the Trojans break their oaths and attack the Achaeans.

l: Juno, The Iliad, BOOK IV.
s: Juno opposes Jove’s suggestion of peace because she wants Troy and Priam’s people destroyed. She argues that Minerva should provoke the Trojans into breaking their oaths.

l: Minerva, The Iliad, BOOK IV.
s: Minerva eagerly descends from Olympus after Jove orders her to make the Trojans break their oaths. Taking the form of Laodocus, she persuades Pandarus to shoot Menelaus and later turns the arrow so that it does not strike a mortal part.

l: Menelaus, The Iliad, BOOK IV.
s: Menelaus is wounded by Pandarus’s arrow after serving as the champion in the agreement with the Trojans. He reassures Agamemnon that the wound is not mortal, and Machaon treats him.

l: Agamemnon, The Iliad, BOOK IV.
s: Agamemnon fears that Menelaus has been mortally wounded and mourns the possible failure of the Achaeans’ expedition. He sends Talthybius to summon Machaon and insists that the Trojans will eventually pay for breaking their oaths.

l: Pandarus, The Iliad, BOOK IV.
s: Pandarus, son of Lycaon, is persuaded by Minerva in the form of Laodocus to shoot Menelaus. He takes up his ibex-horn bow, prays to Lycian Apollo, and fires the arrow that wounds Menelaus.

l: Machaon, The Iliad, BOOK IV.
s: Machaon, son of Aesculapius, is summoned by Agamemnon to treat Menelaus. He removes the arrow and applies soothing drugs given by Chiron to Aesculapius.

l: Trojans, The Iliad, BOOK IV.
s: The Trojans are the intended violators of the oaths when Pandarus attacks Menelaus. Their action renews the danger of war with the Achaeans.

l: Achaeans, The Iliad, BOOK IV.
s: The Achaeans have trusted the oaths, sacrifices, drink-offerings, and gestures of fellowship made with the Trojans. Their champion Menelaus is wounded, and their army is placed in danger of renewed fighting.

l: Troy, The Iliad, BOOK IV.
s: Troy is described as the city whose destruction Juno desires and whose continued existence is proposed as part of a possible peace. Jove says that he has greatly respected Troy, Priam, and its people.

l: Ilius, The Iliad, BOOK IV.
s: Ilius is the city Jove says he has respected, though he allows Juno to pursue its destruction. Agamemnon predicts that Ilius, Priam, and Priam’s people will eventually be laid low.

l: Olympus, The Iliad, BOOK IV.
s: Olympus is where the gods sit in council with Jove and look down upon Troy. Minerva descends from its summits to carry out Jove’s command.

l: arrow, The Iliad, BOOK IV.
s: The arrow Pandarus fires passes through Menelaus’s outer belt, cuirass, and inner belt before grazing his skin. Minerva diverts it from a mortal part, and Machaon later removes it.

l: the covenant of peace, The Iliad, BOOK IV.
s: The oaths, sacrifices, drink-offerings, and gestures of fellowship were intended to preserve the agreement between the Trojans and Achaeans. Minerva causes Pandarus to violate them by attacking Menelaus.

l: peace, The Iliad, BOOK IV.
s: Jove considers making peace so that Menelaus can take Helen back while Troy remains inhabited. Juno and Minerva reject this outcome and work to renew the conflict.

l: the Trojan War, The Iliad, BOOK IV.
s: The gods debate whether war should resume after Menelaus and Alexandrus have fought. Pandarus’s attack on Menelaus breaks the agreement and leads toward renewed combat.

l: Pandarus’s attack on Menelaus, The Iliad, BOOK IV.
s: Pandarus’s attack is prompted by Minerva, who promises him honor and Trojan gratitude if he shoots Menelaus. The shot violates the oaths but fails to kill Menelaus because Minerva diverts the arrow.

l: Menelaus’s wound, The Iliad, BOOK IV.
s: Menelaus’s wound bleeds after the arrow passes through his belts and cuirass, causing Agamemnon and the surrounding Achaeans to fear for him. Machaon removes the arrow and treats the injury with soothing drugs.

l: the destruction of Troy, The Iliad, BOOK IV.
s: Juno is determined to sack Troy and its people, while Jove says he would permit her to have her way despite his former respect for Ilius. Agamemnon predicts that Troy will eventually be destroyed as punishment for the Trojans’ treachery.

l: The Iliad, The Iliad, While they were thus busy about Menelaus, the Trojans came
s: Agamemnon rallies the Achaeans and rebukes those who hesitate as the Trojans advance and renew the fighting. He praises Idomeneus, the two Ajaxes, and Nestor, while urging Ulysses, Menestheus, and Diomed to enter the battle. The Achaeans and Trojans then clash in a violent engagement, during which Antilochus, Ajax, Ulysses, and others kill enemy warriors, while many fighters on both sides fall. Apollo encourages the Trojans, Minerva urges the Achaeans forward, and the fighting continues with great losses.

l: Trojans, The Iliad, While they were thus busy about Menelaus, the Trojans came
s: The Trojans put on their armour, advance against the Achaeans, and renew the fight. Apollo urges them to press the attack after Ulysses kills Democoon, but they suffer heavy losses in the ensuing battle.

l: Danaans, The Iliad, While they were thus busy about Menelaus, the Trojans came
s: The Achaeans are rallied by Agamemnon and advance in disciplined silence against the Trojans. They kill several Trojan fighters, including Echepolus, Simoeisius, and Democoon, while also suffering many casualties.

l: Argives, The Iliad, While they were thus busy about Menelaus, the Trojans came
s: Agamemnon urges the Argives not to slacken in their attack and promises that they will take the Trojan city if they fight bravely. The Argives advance and raise a shout after Ulysses kills Democoon.

l: Agamemnon, The Iliad, While they were thus busy about Menelaus, the Trojans came
s: Agamemnon leaves his chariot with Eurymedon and walks among the ranks, encouraging the eager and rebuking those who hesitate. He praises Idomeneus, the two Ajaxes, and Nestor, challenges Ulysses and Diomed to fight, and then rejoices as the armies engage.

l: Ajax son of Telamon, The Iliad, While they were thus busy about Menelaus, the Trojans came
s: Ajax, son of Telamon, leads a large host of foot soldiers into battle. He kills Simoeisius by striking him in the breast with his spear.

l: Nestor, The Iliad, While they were thus busy about Menelaus, the Trojans came
s: Nestor marshals the Pylians, placing the chariots in front and the dependable foot soldiers behind them, while forcing the cowards into the middle. He advises the knights to maintain formation and throw their spears from their chariots rather than engage singly.

l: Ulysses, The Iliad, While they were thus busy about Menelaus, the Trojans came
s: Ulysses is rebuked by Agamemnon for waiting with the Cephallenians, but he answers angrily that he will fight in the foremost ranks. After Leucus is killed, Ulysses enters the fighting and kills Democoon, causing the Trojans to fall back.

l: Diomed, The Iliad, While they were thus busy about Menelaus, the Trojans came
s: Agamemnon reproaches Diomed for standing by his chariot and compares him unfavourably with his father, Tydeus. Diomed accepts the rebuke, tells Sthenelus to be silent, and springs from his chariot to fight.

l: Minerva, The Iliad, While they were thus busy about Menelaus, the Trojans came
s: Minerva inspires the Achaeans and goes among them urging them forward whenever they begin to slacken. She is contrasted with Mars, who inspires the Trojans.

l: Troy, The Iliad, While they were thus busy about Menelaus, the Trojans came
s: Agamemnon says that the Achaeans would soon make the city of Priam fall and sack it if all their leaders fought with the determination of the two Ajaxes. The text does not report the capture of Troy in this unit.

l: battle, The Iliad, While they were thus busy about Menelaus, the Trojans came
s: The battle begins as the Trojan and Achaean ranks meet, with shields and spears clashing and the earth running red with blood. Numerous named warriors are killed, and the fighting remains fierce under the influence of Apollo and Minerva.

l: breaking of the oaths, The Iliad, While they were thus busy about Menelaus, the Trojans came
s: Agamemnon and Idomeneus say that the Trojans broke their covenants and oaths first by attacking the Achaeans. They therefore declare that death and destruction should befall the Trojans.

l: The Iliad, The Iliad, BOOK V.
s: Pallas Minerva strengthens Diomed, who kills many Trojans after Pandarus wounds him. Diomed kills Pandarus and severely wounds Aeneas, whose mother Venus rescues him from the battle. Diomed then wounds Venus when she tries to protect Aeneas, while Apollo hides Aeneas in a cloud. Minerva removes Mars from the fighting, allowing the Achaeans to drive the Trojans back.

l: Pallas Minerva, The Iliad, BOOK V.
s: Pallas Minerva puts courage into Diomed’s heart, strengthens his body, and removes the veil from his eyes so that he can distinguish gods from men. She tells him not to fight any god except Venus, whom he is permitted to wound, and earlier draws Mars away from the battle.

l: Aeneas, The Iliad, BOOK V.
s: Aeneas joins Pandarus in attacking Diomed and drives the chariot during the assault. Diomed strikes him in the hip with a large stone, leaving him near death, but Venus carries him from the battle and Apollo hides him in a cloud.

l: Venus, The Iliad, BOOK V.
s: Venus rescues her wounded son Aeneas by covering him with her garment and carrying him from the fight. When she tries to protect him, Diomed wounds her in the hand, causing immortal blood to flow, and she abandons Aeneas to Apollo.

l: Apollo, The Iliad, BOOK V.
s: Apollo catches Aeneas when Venus drops him after being wounded. He hides Aeneas in a cloud so that the Achaeans will not kill him.

l: Mars, The Iliad, BOOK V.
s: Mars is drawn away from the battle by Pallas Minerva and set down on the banks of the Scamander. His withdrawal allows the Danaans to drive the Trojans back.

l: Trojans, The Iliad, BOOK V.
s: The Trojans are driven back by the Achaeans as Diomed and other Greek leaders kill their warriors. They are frightened when the sons of Dares are defeated, and they suffer further losses when Diomed attacks their ranks.

l: Achaeans, The Iliad, BOOK V.
s: The Achaeans gain ground after Minerva removes Mars from the battle. Their leaders kill many Trojans, and Sthenelus captures Aeneas’s horses for the Achaean side.

l: battle, The Iliad, BOOK V.
s: The battle becomes especially fierce as Diomed cuts through the Trojan ranks and the Achaean leaders kill many opponents. Gods intervene on both sides: Minerva aids Diomed, Mars is removed, Venus rescues Aeneas, and Apollo hides him.

l: Diomed’s wounding by Pandarus, The Iliad, BOOK V.
s: Pandarus wounds Diomed in the shoulder with an arrow that pierces his cuirass, but Sthenelus removes it. Pandarus later strikes Diomed’s shield and breastplate with a spear, yet Diomed remains unharmed enough to kill him.

l: Pandarus’s death, The Iliad, BOOK V.
s: Diomed kills Pandarus by throwing a spear that Minerva guides into his face near the eye. The spear passes through his teeth and tongue, and Pandarus falls dead from the chariot.

l: Aeneas’s wounding, The Iliad, BOOK V.
s: Diomed wounds Aeneas by striking him in the hip with a massive stone. The blow crushes the joint, breaks the sinews, and leaves Aeneas on his knees with darkness covering his eyes.

l: Venus’s rescue of Aeneas, The Iliad, BOOK V.
s: Venus sees Aeneas in danger and throws her arms around him, shielding him with her garment. She carries him out of the fight, but Apollo ultimately takes him and conceals him in a cloud.

l: Venus’s wounding by Diomed, The Iliad, BOOK V.
s: Diomed pursues Venus because Minerva has told him that he may fight her. He pierces the flesh of her hand through her ambrosial robe, causing ichor to pour from the wound and making her drop Aeneas.

l: The Iliad, The Iliad, The goddess went dazed and discomfited away, and Iris, fleet as
s: Venus, wounded by Diomed while rescuing Aeneas, is taken to Olympus by Iris and healed by her mother Dione, while the gods mock her and warn against mortal defiance. Apollo rescues Aeneas, creates a likeness of him, and calls Mars to aid the Trojans; Mars then strengthens the Trojan attack. Hector rallies the Trojans after Sarpedon rebukes him, and the battle intensifies with many deaths on both sides. Tlepolemus and Sarpedon fight in single combat, both are wounded, but Tlepolemus dies while Sarpedon survives and is carried from the field.

l: Venus, The Iliad, The goddess went dazed and discomfited away, and Iris, fleet as
s: Venus is wounded in the wrist by Diomed while carrying Aeneas from the battle. Iris takes her to Olympus, where Dione heals her; Venus tells Dione that the Danaans are now fighting immortals as well as Trojans.

l: Mars, The Iliad, The goddess went dazed and discomfited away, and Iris, fleet as
s: Mars gives Venus his gold-bedizened horses and chariot. At Apollo's urging, he enters the battle in the likeness of Acamas, rallies the Trojans, and covers them in a veil of darkness.

l: Diomed, The Iliad, The goddess went dazed and discomfited away, and Iris, fleet as
s: Diomed wounds Venus and later attacks Aeneas even while Apollo protects him. Apollo drives Diomed back and warns him that mortals cannot match the immortals.

l: Jove, The Iliad, The goddess went dazed and discomfited away, and Iris, fleet as
s: Jove is told that Diomed would now fight even with him. He smiles at Minerva's mockery of Venus and tells Venus to leave warfare to Mars and Minerva.

l: Aeneas, The Iliad, The goddess went dazed and discomfited away, and Iris, fleet as
s: Aeneas is rescued from Diomed by Apollo and taken to Pergamus, where Latona and Diana heal him. Apollo creates a likeness of Aeneas to deceive the fighters, and the restored Aeneas returns to the battle and kills Crethon and Orsilochus.

l: Venus’s wounding by Diomed, The Iliad, The goddess went dazed and discomfited away, and Iris, fleet as
s: Venus, called the Cyprian, is wounded by Diomed in the hand near the wrist while rescuing Aeneas. Dione wipes the ichor from the wound, and the pain leaves her.

l: Danaans, The Iliad, The goddess went dazed and discomfited away, and Iris, fleet as
s: The Danaans stand firm against the Trojan attack, though they retreat when they learn that Mars is with the Trojans. They suffer several losses but continue fighting under the encouragement of their leaders.

l: Achaeans, The Iliad, The goddess went dazed and discomfited away, and Iris, fleet as
s: The Achaeans attack and kill several Trojans, including Deicoon, Pylaemenes, Mydon, and others. They remain compact and unflinching against the Trojans, though Mars and Hector drive some of them back.

l: Trojans, The Iliad, The goddess went dazed and discomfited away, and Iris, fleet as
s: The Trojans are rallied by Mars, Sarpedon, and Hector after Aeneas is thought to have fallen. With Mars among them and Apollo restoring Aeneas, they renew their assault on the Achaeans.

l: Minerva, The Iliad, The goddess went dazed and discomfited away, and Iris, fleet as
s: Minerva helps the Danaans and urges Diomed against Venus. She mocks Venus before Jove and later turns Ulysses away from Sarpedon toward the Lycian soldiers.

l: Apollo, The Iliad, The goddess went dazed and discomfited away, and Iris, fleet as
s: Apollo protects Aeneas from Diomed, removes him to Pergamus, and has Latona and Diana heal him. He creates a likeness of Aeneas and calls Mars into the battle to strengthen the Trojans.

l: Mars's intervention in the battle, The Iliad, The goddess went dazed and discomfited away, and Iris, fleet as
s: Mars enters the battle at Apollo's request, disguised as Acamas. He rallies the Trojans, covers them with darkness, and causes the Danaans to retreat while keeping their faces turned toward the enemy.

l: Sarpedon, The Iliad, The goddess went dazed and discomfited away, and Iris, fleet as
s: Sarpedon rebukes Hector for failing to defend Troy and emphasizes that he has come from Lycia despite leaving behind his wife, infant son, and wealth. He fights Tlepolemus, kills him, and is wounded in the thigh before being carried away and revived from a swoon.

l: Hector, The Iliad, The goddess went dazed and discomfited away, and Iris, fleet as
s: Hector is sternly criticized by Sarpedon for allowing the Trojans and their allies to bear the brunt of the fighting. He responds by rallying the Trojan host, kills Menesthes and Anchialus, and drives toward the Achaeans when he sees Ulysses attacking the Lycians.

l: Lycians, The Iliad, The goddess went dazed and discomfited away, and Iris, fleet as
s: The Lycians fight for Troy under Sarpedon. Ulysses kills several of them after Minerva directs him against their main body, and Hector intervenes when their losses become severe.

l: Troy, The Iliad, The goddess went dazed and discomfited away, and Iris, fleet as
s: Troy is threatened by the renewed Trojan-Achaean fighting, and Sarpedon warns that the city may be sacked if its defenders fail. Aeneas is healed in Pergamus within the city’s sacred sanctuary.

l: the two Ajaxes, The Iliad, The goddess went dazed and discomfited away, and Iris, fleet as
s: The two Ajaxes encourage the Danaans and stand among the leaders who keep them from yielding to the Trojan attack.

l: Ajax son of Telamon, The Iliad, The goddess went dazed and discomfited away, and Iris, fleet as
s: Ajax son of Telamon kills Amphius with a spear through the belt. He tries to strip Amphius's armour but is forced back by the many spears of the Trojans.

l: Ulysses, The Iliad, The goddess went dazed and discomfited away, and Iris, fleet as
s: Ulysses considers pursuing Sarpedon but is redirected by Minerva toward the Lycian ranks. He kills Coeranus, Alastor, Chromius, Alcandrus, Halius, Noemon, and Prytanis before Hector comes against him.

l: Tlepolemus, The Iliad, The goddess went dazed and discomfited away, and Iris, fleet as
s: Tlepolemus, son of Hercules, challenges Sarpedon and boasts of his father's destruction of Ilius. He wounds Sarpedon in the thigh but is struck through the throat and dies.

l: Tlepolemus–Sarpedon duel, The Iliad, The goddess went dazed and discomfited away, and Iris, fleet as
s: Tlepolemus and Sarpedon exchange insults before throwing their spears at the same moment. Sarpedon kills Tlepolemus with a throat wound, while Tlepolemus wounds Sarpedon in the thigh; Sarpedon is carried away alive.

l: battle, The Iliad, The goddess went dazed and discomfited away, and Iris, fleet as
s: The battle shifts when Mars joins the Trojans and Apollo restores Aeneas. Both sides suffer notable losses, while Hector rallies the Trojans and the Achaeans hold their ground or retreat cautiously in the presence of the gods.

l: gods fighting mortals, The Iliad, The goddess went dazed and discomfited away, and Iris, fleet as
s: The unit presents mortals confronting and wounding gods: Diomed wounds Venus and challenges Apollo, while Apollo warns that mortals cannot match immortals. Dione also recalls earlier cases in which Mars, Juno, and Hades suffered injuries from mortals.

l: The Iliad, The Iliad, Now when the goddess Juno saw the Argives thus falling, she said
s: Juno and Minerva intervene because Mars is causing the Argives to fall and the promise that Menelaus would sack Ilius is being endangered. With Jove's approval, Minerva helps Diomed attack Mars, deflecting Mars's spear and guiding Diomed's spear into Mars's stomach. Mars flees wounded to Olympus, where Jove rebukes him and Paeeon heals him. Juno and Minerva then return to Jove's house after stopping Mars's murderous actions.

l: Juno, The Iliad, Now when the goddess Juno saw the Argives thus falling, she said
s: Juno sees the Argives falling and urges Minerva to enter the battle against Mars. She drives her divine horses to Troy, encourages the Argives with a loud battle cry, and later returns with Minerva to Jove's house.

l: Minerva, The Iliad, Now when the goddess Juno saw the Argives thus falling, she said
s: Minerva joins Juno in going to the battle and arms herself with her aegis, helmet, spear, and chariot. She protects Diomed by deflecting Mars's spear, drives Diomed's spear into Mars, and helps stop Mars's murderous actions.

l: Jove, The Iliad, Now when the goddess Juno saw the Argives thus falling, she said
s: Jove approves Juno's plan to attack Mars and tells her to set Minerva against him. When Mars complains after being wounded, Jove rebukes him but orders Paeeon to heal him.

l: Mars, The Iliad, Now when the goddess Juno saw the Argives thus falling, she said
s: Mars is fighting on the side of the Trojans and has destroyed many Achaeans. Minerva enables Diomed to wound him in the stomach, after which Mars cries out, flees to Olympus, complains to Jove, and is healed by Paeeon.

l: Diomed, The Iliad, Now when the goddess Juno saw the Argives thus falling, she said
s: Diomed is suffering from the wound given him by Pandarus but continues to fight. Encouraged and protected by Minerva, he wounds Mars with his spear and drives him from the battle.

l: Argives, The Iliad, Now when the goddess Juno saw the Argives thus falling, she said
s: The Argives are suffering heavy losses while Mars fights against them. Juno calls them shameful for losing courage, and her speech restores their fighting spirit.

l: Trojans, The Iliad, Now when the goddess Juno saw the Argives thus falling, she said
s: The Trojans are fighting at the ships and are being aided by Mars. They are struck with panic when Mars gives a terrifying cry after Diomed wounds him.

l: Troy, The Iliad, Now when the goddess Juno saw the Argives thus falling, she said
s: Troy is the place where Juno and Minerva arrive after traveling from Olympus. Near Troy, at the meeting of the Simois and Scamander, Juno hides the divine horses before the goddesses enter the battle.

l: Olympus, The Iliad, Now when the goddess Juno saw the Argives thus falling, she said
s: Olympus is the home of the gods and the place where Jove sits on the highest ridges. Mars flees there after being wounded and sits beside Jove in great pain.

l: battle, The Iliad, Now when the goddess Juno saw the Argives thus falling, she said
s: The fighting is intensified by Mars's intervention on the Trojan side and by Juno and Minerva's support for the Argives. Diomed's attack on Mars temporarily stops Mars's murderous activity in the battle.

l: divine intervention in the battle, The Iliad, Now when the goddess Juno saw the Argives thus falling, she said
s: Juno and Minerva enter the fighting directly, encourage the Argives, and assist Diomed against Mars. Minerva conceals herself with the helmet of Hades, deflects Mars's spear, and guides Diomed's spear into him.

l: wounding of Mars, The Iliad, Now when the goddess Juno saw the Argives thus falling, she said
s: Diomed wounds Mars in the stomach after Minerva deflects Mars's attack and guides Diomed's spear. Mars cries out, flees to Olympus, and is healed by Paeeon with pain-killing herbs.

l: The Iliad, The Iliad, BOOK VI.
s: The war between the Trojans and Achaeans surges across the plain, with many warriors killed on both sides. Diomed kills Axylus and his squire, while Menelaus captures Adrestus but kills him after Agamemnon urges that no Trojan be spared. Helenus tells Hector and Aeneas to rally the Trojans and advises Hector to ask the women of Ilius to pray to Minerva. Hector rallies the Trojan host and goes to Ilius to call for prayers and sacrifices.

l: Diomed, The Iliad, BOOK VI.
s: Diomed kills Axylus, a wealthy and well-loved man from Arisbe, as well as Axylus's squire and charioteer, Calesius.

l: Hector, The Iliad, BOOK VI.
s: Hector rallies the Trojans after Helenus advises him to strengthen their forces. He goes to Ilius to tell the elders and women to pray to the gods and vow sacrifices.

l: Trojans, The Iliad, BOOK VI.
s: The Trojans are driven toward Ilius by the Achaeans until Helenus, Hector, and Aeneas help rally them. They turn and face the Achaeans again while prayers and sacrifices are prepared in Ilius.

l: Achaeans, The Iliad, BOOK VI.
s: The Achaeans gain ground and kill many Trojans, but they stop their attack when the Trojans suddenly rally. Nestor urges them to kill as many enemies as possible and postpone stripping the dead until later.

l: Agamemnon, The Iliad, BOOK VI.
s: Agamemnon rebukes Menelaus for considering mercy toward Adrestus and urges that no Trojan, including unborn children, be spared. He then kills Adrestus by striking him in the flank.

l: Menelaus, The Iliad, BOOK VI.
s: Menelaus captures Adrestus after Adrestus's horses run into a tamarisk bush and throw him from his chariot. He initially considers sparing him for ransom, but Agamemnon persuades him otherwise.

l: Helenus, The Iliad, BOOK VI.
s: Helenus, described as the wisest of augurs, tells Hector and Aeneas to rally the Trojans. He directs Hector to ask the women of Ilius to offer a robe and twelve yearling heifers to Minerva for protection.

l: Aeneas, The Iliad, BOOK VI.
s: Aeneas is identified by Helenus as one of the mainstays of the Trojans and Lycians in both fighting and counsel. Helenus tells him to hold his ground and rally the Trojan forces.

l: Ilius, The Iliad, BOOK VI.
s: Ilius is the city toward which the Trojans retreat and the place Hector enters to seek support. Its acropolis contains Minerva's temple, where the women are instructed to pray for the city's safety.

l: battle, The Iliad, BOOK VI.
s: The war rages between the Trojans and Achaeans across the plain between the streams of Simois and Xanthus. The fighting shifts back and forth as both sides kill one another and attempt to rally their forces.

l: The Iliad, The Iliad, Then Glaucus son of Hippolochus, and the son of Tydeus went into
s: Diomed and Glaucus son of Hippolochus meet in single combat, discover that their families are connected by old hospitality, exchange armor, and agree to avoid fighting one another. Hector returns to Troy and urges his mother to offer prayers and a robe to Minerva so that Diomed will be stopped. He rebukes Paris, then meets Andromache and their child, but insists that he must return to battle despite foreseeing Troy’s destruction and Andromache’s possible captivity. Paris arms himself and joins Hector, promising to follow him into the fighting.

l: Diomed, The Iliad, Then Glaucus son of Hippolochus, and the son of Tydeus went into
s: Diomed challenges Glaucus son of Hippolochus and asks whether he is a mortal or an immortal. After learning of Glaucus’s descent and his family’s ties to Oeneus, he recognizes him as an old friend of his father’s house, agrees to avoid fighting him, and exchanges armor with him.

l: Glaucus, The Iliad, Then Glaucus son of Hippolochus, and the son of Tydeus went into
s: Glaucus tells Diomed the history of his descent from Sisyphus, Bellerophon, and Hippolochus. He agrees to friendship with Diomed and exchanges his golden armor for Diomed’s bronze armor, which is described as greatly less valuable.

l: Hector, The Iliad, Then Glaucus son of Hippolochus, and the son of Tydeus went into
s: Hector returns to Troy, urges the women to pray to Minerva, rebukes Paris for remaining away from battle, and visits his wife and child. He refuses to shirk the fighting, predicts that Ilius will one day be destroyed, and parts from Andromache to return to battle.

l: Andromache, The Iliad, Then Glaucus son of Hippolochus, and the son of Tydeus went into
s: Andromache meets Hector at the Scaean gates with their child and begs him to stay, recounting how Achilles killed her father and brothers and how she fears becoming a captive widow. Hector comforts her but refuses to remain, and she returns home weeping.

l: Alexandrus, The Iliad, Then Glaucus son of Hippolochus, and the son of Tydeus went into
s: Paris is found in his house tending his armor while the fighting continues outside. After Hector rebukes him, he arms himself, catches up with Hector, and says that he will follow him into battle.

l: Helen, The Iliad, Then Glaucus son of Hippolochus, and the son of Tydeus went into
s: Helen is in Paris’s house with her women when Hector arrives. She condemns herself and Paris for the suffering caused to the Trojans, acknowledges Hector’s burden, and urges him to rest, but Hector declines.

l: Troy, The Iliad, Then Glaucus son of Hippolochus, and the son of Tydeus went into
s: Troy is under severe pressure from the Achaeans, and its women pray to Minerva for protection. Hector fears that the city will be destroyed, while Paris’s absence from the fighting is blamed for adding to the Trojans’ suffering.

l: Ilius, The Iliad, Then Glaucus son of Hippolochus, and the son of Tydeus went into
s: Ilius is the city Hector helps defend, and Hector is described as its chief guardian. Hector tells Andromache that mighty Ilius will eventually be destroyed with Priam and Priam’s people.

l: Achaeans, The Iliad, Then Glaucus son of Hippolochus, and the son of Tydeus went into
s: The Achaeans press hard around Troy and fight in great force. Hector expects them to attack him and fears that one of them may eventually take Andromache into captivity.

l: Trojans, The Iliad, Then Glaucus son of Hippolochus, and the son of Tydeus went into
s: The Trojans are being hard pressed and suffer while fighting around their city. Their women pray for protection, and they criticize Paris for failing to take his proper share in the battle.

l: single combat between Diomed and Glaucus, The Iliad, Then Glaucus son of Hippolochus, and the son of Tydeus went into
s: Diomed and Glaucus meet between the opposing hosts and prepare to fight. Their combat ends without violence when they discover their inherited ties of hospitality and decide to avoid one another’s spears.

l: exchange of armor between Diomed and Glaucus, The Iliad, Then Glaucus son of Hippolochus, and the son of Tydeus went into
s: Diomed and Glaucus exchange armor so that everyone present will know of the old ties between their families. Glaucus gives golden armor valued at a hundred head of cattle and receives bronze armor valued at nine.

l: friendship between Diomed and Glaucus, The Iliad, Then Glaucus son of Hippolochus, and the son of Tydeus went into
s: Diomed and Glaucus establish friendship after learning that Oeneus once entertained Bellerophon. They pledge to be hosts to one another in Argos and Lycia and to avoid fighting each other even during a general engagement.

l: Hector’s appeal to the Trojans, The Iliad, Then Glaucus son of Hippolochus, and the son of Tydeus went into
s: Hector directs his mother and the matrons to pray to Minerva and offer the finest robe and twelve unyoked heifers. The prayer asks Minerva to pity Troy and keep Diomed away from the city, but Minerva does not grant it.

l: Hector and Andromache’s parting, The Iliad, Then Glaucus son of Hippolochus, and the son of Tydeus went into
s: Hector and Andromache part at the city wall after she begs him to protect her and their child by staying. Hector says that honor and duty require him to fight, comforts her with the thought that no one dies before the appointed time, and returns to battle while she goes home mourning.

l: the Trojan War, The Iliad, Then Glaucus son of Hippolochus, and the son of Tydeus went into
s: The Trojan War continues with the Achaeans attacking and the Trojans defending their city. The unit presents both battlefield encounters and the private grief of Hector, Andromache, Helen, and the people of Troy.

l: captivity of Andromache, The Iliad, Then Glaucus son of Hippolochus, and the son of Tydeus went into
s: Hector foresees that Andromache may be taken captive if the Achaeans destroy Ilius. He imagines her being carried weeping to Argos, forced to weave or fetch water, and treated brutally by a mistress or taskmaster.

l: Hector’s child, The Iliad, Then Glaucus son of Hippolochus, and the son of Tydeus went into
s: Hector’s young son, called Scamandrius by Hector and Astyanax by the people, is frightened by his father’s armor and helmet plume. Hector removes the helmet, embraces and kisses the child, and prays that he will become a strong and renowned ruler of Ilius.

l: The Iliad, The Iliad, BOOK VII.
s: Hector challenges the Achaeans to single combat, and Ajax is chosen to face him. Hector and Ajax fight fiercely until nightfall, when heralds stop them; they exchange gifts and part with mutual respect. Nestor proposes that the armies burn their dead and build a wall and trench around the Achaean ships. The Trojans offer to return Paris’s wealth but refuse to surrender Helen, while the Achaeans reject the offer and agree only to a truce for burying the dead.

l: Hector, The Iliad, BOOK VII.
s: Hector rallies the Trojans, challenges the Achaeans to single combat, and fights Ajax until nightfall. Ajax wounds him and knocks him down with a great stone, but Apollo raises him; Hector then agrees to stop fighting, exchanges gifts with Ajax, and returns safely to Ilius.

l: Trojans, The Iliad, BOOK VII.
s: The Trojans are encouraged when Hector and Alexandrus return to the fighting, but they tremble when Ajax comes forward. They hold a council in which Antenor urges them to give up Helen, while Alexandrus refuses to surrender her; they later gather and burn their dead.

l: Achaeans, The Iliad, BOOK VII.
s: The Achaeans are challenged to provide a champion for Hector, and Ajax is chosen by lot. They reject the Trojan offer of treasure without Helen, agree to let both armies burn their dead, and begin planning defenses around their ships.

l: Minerva, The Iliad, BOOK VII.
s: Minerva comes down from Olympus after seeing the Trojans make havoc among the Achaeans. She meets Apollo and agrees to end the day’s fighting by having Hector challenge an Achaean champion; she later watches the armies in the likeness of a vulture.

l: Apollo, The Iliad, BOOK VII.
s: Apollo meets Minerva and proposes that Hector challenge an Achaean champion so that the fighting can be suspended for the day. During the combat, Apollo raises Hector after Ajax’s stone knocks him down.

l: Jove, The Iliad, BOOK VII.
s: Jove is invoked as witness to the proposed terms of single combat and to the prayers of both armies. Agamemnon later calls Jove witness to the agreement allowing the dead to be burned.

l: Agamemnon, The Iliad, BOOK VII.
s: Agamemnon prevents Menelaus from fighting Hector and joins the group of Achaean leaders who offer themselves as champions. He sacrifices a five-year-old bull for Ajax and the Achaeans, gives Ajax special portions of meat, and rejects the Trojan offer except for the proposed truce to burn the dead.

l: Menelaus, The Iliad, BOOK VII.
s: Menelaus rebukes the Achaeans for refusing Hector’s challenge and begins to arm himself to fight. Agamemnon stops him, judging Hector too strong for him; Menelaus is also the husband whose wife the Trojans refuse to surrender.

l: Ajax son of Telamon, The Iliad, BOOK VII.
s: Ajax is selected by lot to fight Hector and approaches him with a massive shield. He wounds Hector in the neck and knocks him down with a large stone, then accepts the end of the combat at nightfall and exchanges gifts with Hector.

l: Nestor, The Iliad, BOOK VII.
s: Nestor rebukes the Achaeans for fearing Hector and recalls how he once defeated Ereuthalion when he was young. He proposes choosing a champion by lot and later advises the Achaeans to burn their dead and build a wall and trench around their ships.

l: Helen, The Iliad, BOOK VII.
s: Helen is the wedded wife of Menelaus and the woman whose presence is the subject of the quarrel. Antenor urges the Trojans to give her back, but Alexandrus refuses to surrender her.

l: Ilius, The Iliad, BOOK VII.
s: Ilius is the city to which Hector returns after the combat and where the Trojans hold their council. Hector’s proposed fame includes having his defeated opponent’s armour hung in the temple of Apollo there.

l: single combat between Hector and Ajax, The Iliad, BOOK VII.
s: Hector challenges the Achaeans to single combat, offering the victor the opponent’s armour while requiring the defeated man’s body to be returned for burial. Ajax is chosen to face him; they exchange spear thrusts and stones until nightfall, when heralds stop them before either can finish the fight.

l: exchange of presents between Hector and Ajax, The Iliad, BOOK VII.
s: After their combat is stopped, Hector gives Ajax a silver-studded sword with its sheath and leathern baldric. Ajax gives Hector a purple-dyed girdle, and they part in friendship while both armies rejoice that their champion has returned safely.

l: burial and burning of the dead, The Iliad, BOOK VII.
s: After the armies agree to a truce, the Trojans and Achaeans gather their dead, wash away the blood, mourn them, and place them on pyres. The Trojans burn their dead silently by Priam’s order, and the Achaeans do likewise before returning to their ships.

l: Achaean wall, The Iliad, BOOK VII.
s: Nestor proposes that the Achaeans build a high wall with gates around their ships and dig a deep trench outside it. The defenses are intended to shelter the Achaeans and prevent Trojan horsemen and foot soldiers from attacking them.

l: The Iliad, The Iliad, Now in the twilight when it was not yet dawn, chosen bands of the
s: The Achaeans gather at twilight, build a common barrow, and construct a fortified wall around their ships with gates, a trench, and stakes. The gods observe and marvel at the work. Neptune objects that the Achaeans built the wall without offering hecatombs and fears it will rival the wall he and Phoebus Apollo built for Laomedon. Jove replies that Neptune can destroy the Achaean wall and erase it after the Achaeans return home.

l: Achaeans, The Iliad, Now in the twilight when it was not yet dawn, chosen bands of the
s: The Achaeans gather around the pyre, build one barrow in common, and construct a high wall to shelter themselves and their ships. They add strong gates, dig a deep and wide trench, and plant the trench with stakes.

l: Achaean wall, The Iliad, Now in the twilight when it was not yet dawn, chosen bands of the
s: The Achaean wall is built around the ships with strong gates, a deep trench, and stakes. Neptune objects that it was built without offerings to the gods, while Jove says it can later be shattered, cast into the sea, and covered with sand.

l: gods, The Iliad, Now in the twilight when it was not yet dawn, chosen bands of the
s: The gods sit beside Jove and marvel at the great work of the Achaeans. Neptune speaks against the wall because the Achaeans built it without offering hecatombs to the gods.

l: Jove, The Iliad, Now in the twilight when it was not yet dawn, chosen bands of the
s: Jove is displeased by Neptune's remarks and answers that Neptune can destroy the Achaean wall after the Achaeans have gone home with their ships. He says the wall can be utterly effaced by casting it into the sea and covering the beach with sand.

l: Neptune, The Iliad, Now in the twilight when it was not yet dawn, chosen bands of the
s: Neptune, lord of the earthquake, objects that the Achaeans built a wall around their ships and dug a trench without taking the gods into their counsel or offering hecatombs. He fears that the wall's fame will rival the wall he and Phoebus Apollo built for Laomedon, and Jove tells him that he can later destroy it.

l: The Iliad, The Iliad, Thus did they converse, and by sunset the work of the Achaeans
s: By sunset, the Achaeans completed their work, slaughtered oxen, and ate supper at their tents. Ships from Lemnos brought wine sent by Eueneus the son of Jason, and the Achaeans exchanged bronze, iron, hides, heifers, and captives for it. The Achaeans feasted through the night, while the Trojans and their allies did likewise in the city. Jove then roared with portentous thunder, causing fear, and the people poured out their wine and made offerings before going to sleep.

l: Danaans, The Iliad, Thus did they converse, and by sunset the work of the Achaeans
s: The Achaeans completed their work by sunset, slaughtered oxen, and ate supper at their tents. They bought wine using bronze, iron, hides, whole heifers, and captives, then feasted through the night. When Jove thundered, they poured wine onto the ground and made offerings before sleeping.

l: Eueneus the son of Jason, The Iliad, Thus did they converse, and by sunset the work of the Achaeans
s: Eueneus the son of Jason sent ships from Lemnos carrying wine. He was born to Jason by Hypsipyle and sent the wine specially to the sons of Atreus, Agamemnon and Menelaus.

l: wine, The Iliad, Thus did they converse, and by sunset the work of the Achaeans
s: Wine came from Lemnos in many ships and was supplied by Eueneus the son of Jason. The Achaeans bought it with various goods and captives, but after Jove's thunder they poured it onto the ground and did not drink until they had made offerings.

l: banquet, The Iliad, Thus did they converse, and by sunset the work of the Achaeans
s: The Achaeans spread a goodly banquet and feasted through the whole night. The Trojans and their allies also feasted in the city.

l: Trojans, The Iliad, Thus did they converse, and by sunset the work of the Achaeans
s: The Trojans and their allies feasted through the night in the city. Jove's portentous thunder also caused fear among them.

l: Jove, The Iliad, Thus did they converse, and by sunset the work of the Achaeans
s: Jove boded ill for the Achaeans, the Trojans, and their allies by roaring with portentous thunder. His thunder caused pale fear, leading them to pour wine onto the ground and make offerings to the most mighty son of Saturn.

l: The Iliad, The Iliad, BOOK VIII.
s: Jove forbids the gods from aiding either side, then watches from Ida as the Trojans and Achaeans fight. At midday he tips the balance toward the Trojans, who drive the Achaeans back toward their trench and ships. Diomed rescues Nestor but retreats under Jove’s thunder, while Hector loses two charioteers and disables Teucer. Agamemnon encourages the Danaans, and the Achaeans briefly rally before Hector again forces them back.

l: Jove, The Iliad, BOOK VIII.
s: Jove forbids the gods from interfering in the battle and threatens to punish anyone who helps the Trojans or Danaans. From Ida he tips his golden scales in favor of the Trojans, sends thunder and lightning against the Achaeans, answers Agamemnon’s prayer with an eagle portent, and repeatedly strengthens the Trojans.

l: the gods, The Iliad, BOOK VIII.
s: The gods assemble on Olympus and hear Jove forbid them to aid either side. They are frightened into silence, though Minerva speaks for the suffering Danaans, and Juno later urges Neptune to help them.

l: Minerva, The Iliad, BOOK VIII.
s: Minerva says that the gods should at least offer useful advice to the Argives so that they do not all perish. Jove reassures her that he is not truly angry and wishes to be kind to her.

l: Juno, The Iliad, BOOK VIII.
s: Juno is enraged by the Trojans’ success and urges Neptune to help the dying Danaans. She also puts it into Agamemnon’s mind to encourage the Achaeans, and Jove later promises that she will have her way in the end.

l: Trojans, The Iliad, BOOK VIII.
s: The Trojans arm themselves and fight eagerly for their wives and children. With Jove’s aid they gain the advantage, drive the Achaeans through the trench, and threaten to burn the ships.

l: Argives, The Iliad, BOOK VIII.
s: The Achaeans arm themselves and fight the Trojans, but Jove’s favor turns against them at midday. They retreat in fear toward their ships, rally briefly after Agamemnon’s prayer, and are driven back again by Hector.

l: Danaans, The Iliad, BOOK VIII.
s: The Danaans suffer heavy losses and are pressed by Hector and the Trojans. Agamemnon prays that they may at least escape with their lives, and Jove grants that his people should live rather than die.

l: Achaeans, The Iliad, BOOK VIII.
s: Agamemnon calls the Argives cowardly and urges them to fight more bravely. They respond to the eagle portent from Jove and attack the Trojans with renewed force.

l: Hector, The Iliad, BOOK VIII.
s: Hector leads the Trojan advance under Jove’s favor, kills or pursues the hindmost Achaeans, and boasts that he will reach and burn their ships. Diomed kills his charioteer Eniopeus, Teucer kills Archeptolemus, and Hector then disables Teucer with a stone before driving the Achaeans back to the trench.

l: Diomed, The Iliad, BOOK VIII.
s: Diomed responds to Nestor’s danger, takes Nestor into his chariot, and attacks Hector. After Jove’s thunderbolt frightens the horses, Diomed reluctantly retreats, killing Agelaus during the renewed Achaean advance.

l: Nestor, The Iliad, BOOK VIII.
s: Nestor’s horse is disabled by an arrow from Alexandrus, leaving him exposed to Hector. Diomed rescues him by taking him into his chariot, and Nestor urges Diomed to retreat when Jove shows that Hector will prevail.

l: Ulysses, The Iliad, BOOK VIII.
s: Ulysses ignores Diomed’s call to help defend Nestor and flees onward toward the Achaean ships.

l: Agamemnon, The Iliad, BOOK VIII.
s: Agamemnon is among the Achaeans who initially retreat, then receives Juno’s prompting to encourage them. He prays to Jove for the Achaeans’ survival, praises Teucer’s shooting, and promises him a great reward if the city of Ilius is sacked.

l: Ajax son of Telamon, The Iliad, BOOK VIII.
s: Ajax son of Telamon fights among the leading Achaeans and shelters his fallen brother Teucer beneath his shield. His ship stands at one end of the Achaean line.

l: Teucer, The Iliad, BOOK VIII.
s: Teucer kills several Trojans with his bow while taking cover behind Ajax son of Telamon’s shield. He twice misses Hector, kills Gorgythion and Archeptolemus instead, and is then struck by Hector’s stone, which breaks the sinew of his arm and makes him drop his bow.

l: Olympus, The Iliad, BOOK VIII.
s: Olympus is the place where Jove calls the gods into council and forbids them to interfere. Juno later makes high Olympus quake with her rage.

l: Ida, The Iliad, BOOK VIII.
s: Jove travels to Ida, reaches Gargarus, and watches the city of Troy and the Achaean ships from its heights.

l: Troy, The Iliad, BOOK VIII.
s: Troy is the city whose warriors fight to defend their wives and children. The Trojans emerge from its open gates and later threaten to drive the Achaeans away and burn their ships.

l: Ilius, The Iliad, BOOK VIII.
s: Ilius is the city into which the Trojans might have been penned, according to Hector’s boast. Agamemnon promises Teucer a reward if the Achaeans sack it.

l: ships of the Achaeans, The Iliad, BOOK VIII.
s: The Achaean ships are the refuge toward which the defeated Achaeans flee. Hector aims to reach them and burn them, while Agamemnon uses Ulysses’ ship as a central place from which to rally the army.

l: the city wall of Ilius, The Iliad, BOOK VIII.
s: The Trojan wall is the wall of Ilius that Hector says will not stop his fury. He boasts that his horses will spring lightly over the Achaeans’ defenses, while the text later describes the Achaeans retreating through their own trench.

l: trench, The Iliad, BOOK VIII.
s: The trench separates the Achaeans from the advancing Trojans. Hector drives the Achaeans through it, and many are killed as they pass its stakes.

l: the battle, The Iliad, BOOK VIII.
s: The battle is initially even through the morning, with heavy fighting and bloodshed on both sides. At midday Jove’s scales turn the outcome toward the Trojans, though the Achaeans briefly rally before Hector restores the Trojan advance.

l: Jove’s prohibition, The Iliad, BOOK VIII.
s: Jove’s prohibition commands every god and goddess not to help either the Trojans or the Danaans. He threatens to beat or cast down anyone who acts independently.

l: the Trojans’ advance, The Iliad, BOOK VIII.
s: The Trojans’ advance begins after Jove tips the scales in their favor and sends thunder against the Achaeans. Hector leads them through the battle, across the trench, and toward the Achaean ships, but the advance is briefly checked by the Achaean rally before continuing.

l: The Iliad, The Iliad, Juno when she saw them had pity upon them, and at once said to
s: Juno and Minerva pity the dying Danaans and prepare to intervene against Hector, but Jove orders Iris to turn them back and threatens them with punishment. Juno and Minerva withdraw to Olympus, where Jove declares that Hector will continue fighting until he rouses Achilles at the ships over Patroclus’s body. Hector leads the Trojans from the ships, orders provisions and watchfires, and predicts that the Argives will suffer heavily at dawn. The Trojans establish a large night watch between Ilius, the ships, and the river Xanthus while the Achaeans remain in danger.

l: Juno, The Iliad, Juno when she saw them had pity upon them, and at once said to
s: Juno pities the dying Danaans and urges Minerva to consider helping them against Hector. She obeys Minerva by harnessing the horses, but turns them back when Iris delivers Jove’s threat. At Olympus, she says that she and Minerva will refrain from fighting but will give useful suggestions to the Argives.

l: Minerva, The Iliad, Juno when she saw them had pity upon them, and at once said to
s: Minerva wants Hector to die in his own land and complains that Jove favors Thetis and Achilles while disregarding the aid she gave Jove’s son during his labours. She arms herself and sets out with Juno, but withdraws after Iris warns that Jove will punish her. At Olympus, she remains silent and furious while brooding mischief against the Trojans.

l: Jove, The Iliad, Juno when she saw them had pity upon them, and at once said to
s: Jove sees Juno and Minerva setting out and sends Iris to order them back, threatening to lame their horses, destroy their chariot, and strike them with lightning. At Olympus, he asserts that all the gods together cannot overcome his power and says that Hector will continue fighting until he rouses Achilles at the ships over Patroclus’s body. He permits Juno and Minerva to advise the Argives but insists that the Argives will suffer heavily.

l: Hector, The Iliad, Juno when she saw them had pity upon them, and at once said to
s: Hector’s attack causes great harm to the Achaeans, and Juno and Minerva fear his intolerable fury. After darkness stops the fighting, he leads the Trojans away from the ships, holds a council, and orders preparations for a night watch. He predicts that the Argives will suffer at dawn and challenges Diomed to meet him in battle.

l: Juno and Minerva, The Iliad, Juno when she saw them had pity upon them, and at once said to
s: Juno and Minerva set out together to help the dying Danaans and confront Hector, but Jove prevents them through Iris’s warning. They return to Olympus and sit apart from Jove, angry at his treatment of them. They agree not to fight directly against his will, though they intend to give the Argives useful advice.

l: Argives, The Iliad, Juno when she saw them had pity upon them, and at once said to
s: The Achaeans are dying and have been driven back toward their ships by Hector and the Trojans. Jove predicts that many of them will be destroyed before Achilles is roused. They remain threatened through the night as the Trojans guard against their escape by sea.

l: Trojans, The Iliad, Juno when she saw them had pity upon them, and at once said to
s: The Trojans follow Hector back from the ships, prepare food and supplies, and offer sacrifices to the immortals. They kindle watchfires across the plain and remain confident while planning to renew the attack at dawn. The gods do not accept their sacrifices because they hate Ilius, Priam, and Priam’s people.

l: the gods, The Iliad, Juno when she saw them had pity upon them, and at once said to
s: The gods witness the conflict from Olympus and are divided by the war. Jove restrains Juno and Minerva, while the gods refuse the Trojans’ sacrifices because they hate Ilius and Priam’s people. The mighty lord of the earthquake helps Jove by unyoking his horses when Jove arrives at Olympus.

l: Achilles, The Iliad, Juno when she saw them had pity upon them, and at once said to
s: Achilles is the son of Peleus and is being honored by Thetis, whom Jove allows to have her way. Jove says that Hector will continue fighting until he rouses Achilles when the Achaeans are in dire straits at their ships over Patroclus’s body.

l: Olympus, The Iliad, Juno when she saw them had pity upon them, and at once said to
s: Olympus is the home of the gods and is reached by Juno and Minerva after Iris turns them back. Jove enters its assembly, sits on his golden throne, and causes Olympus to reel beneath him. Juno and Minerva sit apart from him in anger.

l: Ilius, The Iliad, Juno when she saw them had pity upon them, and at once said to
s: Ilius is the city of Priam and the Trojans. Hector orders the city’s youths and grey-bearded men to camp on its walls and its women to light fires in their houses. The Trojan watchfires shine across the plain before Ilius during the night.

l: ships of the Achaeans, The Iliad, Juno when she saw them had pity upon them, and at once said to
s: The Achaeans’ ships are the focus of Hector’s attack and the place where the Achaeans are in dire straits. Hector orders the Trojans to prevent the Achaeans from escaping by sea and plans to renew the fighting at the ships at dawn. Jove says Hector will fight there until he rouses Achilles over Patroclus’s body.

l: watchfires, The Iliad, Juno when she saw them had pity upon them, and at once said to
s: Hector orders the Trojans to gather much wood and burn watchfires whose light may reach heaven. The fires are kindled across the plain, with about fifty men sitting by each, and they shine between the ships and the river Xanthus throughout the night.

l: Hector’s council, The Iliad, Juno when she saw them had pity upon them, and at once said to
s: Hector’s council takes place in an open space near the river after the Trojans leave the ships. The Trojans sit on the ground and hear Hector order preparations for food, sacrifices, watchfires, and a guarded night camp. He also announces his intention to resume the attack at daybreak.

l: the Trojan night watch, The Iliad, Juno when she saw them had pity upon them, and at once said to
s: The Trojan night watch includes youths and grey-bearded men camping on the walls, women keeping fires in their houses, and warriors stationed by numerous watchfires. Its purpose is to prevent the Achaeans from escaping by sea or entering the city by surprise.

l: the Trojan War, The Iliad, Juno when she saw them had pity upon them, and at once said to
s: Juno and Minerva initially intend to return to the battle against Hector, but Jove forbids them from fighting. Darkness ends the fighting for the day, and Hector orders the Trojans to prepare to resume fierce war at the Achaeans’ ships at dawn.

l: the death of Patroclus, The Iliad, Juno when she saw them had pity upon them, and at once said to
s: Jove refers to Patroclus’s body as the point over which the Achaeans and Hector will be fighting at the ships. The text does not describe the death itself in this unit.

l: the Argives’ destruction, The Iliad, Juno when she saw them had pity upon them, and at once said to
s: Jove tells Juno that she will see the son of Saturn destroying large numbers of the Argives. Hector predicts that Diomed and many other Argives will fall at dawn, while Juno and Minerva pity the Danaans who are already perishing.

l: divine intervention in the Trojan War, The Iliad, Juno when she saw them had pity upon them, and at once said to
s: Divine intervention shapes the fighting when Jove sends Iris to prevent Juno and Minerva from aiding the Achaeans. Jove also declares that Hector’s continued fighting and the eventual rousing of Achilles are decreed, while Juno and Minerva remain limited to offering advice to the Argives.

l: The Iliad, The Iliad, BOOK IX.
s: Agamemnon calls an Achaean council after the Trojans threaten the ships and proposes abandoning the war, but Diomed rejects this and Nestor urges the leaders to seek wise counsel. Nestor reminds Agamemnon that his quarrel with Achilles caused the crisis, so Agamemnon offers extensive gifts, Briseis, a marriage alliance, and cities as amends. Nestor sends Phoenix, Ajax, Ulysses, and heralds as an embassy to Achilles, who receives them hospitably in his tent with Patroclus. Ulysses recounts the danger to the Achaeans and repeats Agamemnon’s offers, urging Achilles to put aside his anger and save the fleet.

l: Achilles, The Iliad, BOOK IX.
s: Achilles remains apart from the fighting in his tent, where he plays a lyre and sings of heroes with Patroclus. He welcomes the embassy, entertains its members, and listens as Ulysses urges him to return to battle by recounting the danger to the Achaeans and Agamemnon’s promised gifts.

l: Agamemnon, The Iliad, BOOK IX.
s: Agamemnon despairs after the Trojan advance and initially tells the Achaeans to sail home. After Nestor reproves him for having angered Achilles, he admits his wrong and offers extensive gifts and honors to make amends.

l: Ulysses, The Iliad, BOOK IX.
s: Ulysses goes with Phoenix and Ajax as an envoy to Achilles. He describes the Trojan threat to the ships, repeats Agamemnon’s offers, and urges Achilles to abandon his anger and save the Achaeans.

l: Ajax son of Telamon, The Iliad, BOOK IX.
s: Ajax is chosen to accompany Phoenix and Ulysses on the embassy to Achilles. At Achilles’ tent, he helps signal that it is time for Ulysses to make the appeal.

l: Phoenix, The Iliad, BOOK IX.
s: Phoenix is appointed by Nestor to lead the embassy to Achilles, with Ajax and Ulysses following him. He travels with them to Achilles’ ships and tent.

l: Patroclus, The Iliad, BOOK IX.
s: Patroclus is with Achilles while Achilles plays the lyre. He helps prepare the meal for the envoys by tending the fire, roasting the meat, and distributing the food.

l: Nestor, The Iliad, BOOK IX.
s: Nestor advises the Achaeans to keep watch, feast, and seek prudent counsel during the crisis. He reproves Agamemnon for taking Briseis from Achilles, recommends gifts and conciliatory words, and names the members of the embassy.

l: Hector, The Iliad, BOOK IX.
s: Hector rages near the Achaean ships, confident that Jove supports him. He vows to destroy the ships and make havoc of the Achaeans, and Ulysses warns that he may soon come within Achilles’ reach.

l: Achaeans, The Iliad, BOOK IX.
s: Agamemnon’s army is frightened and in despair as the Trojans press toward the ships. Its sentinels are stationed between the trench and the wall, while its leaders seek Achilles’ help to prevent destruction.

l: Trojans, The Iliad, BOOK IX.
s: The Trojans camp close to the Achaean ships and wall and light watchfires throughout their host. They believe that nothing can prevent them from attacking the fleet.

l: Jove, The Iliad, BOOK IX.
s: Jove is said to have promised Agamemnon that Troy would fall, but Agamemnon believes that this promise has been withdrawn. Jove is also said to have destroyed many Achaeans and to have shown favor to Achilles, while his lightning on the Trojan right encourages Hector.

l: Briseis, The Iliad, BOOK IX.
s: Briseis is the girl whom Agamemnon took from Achilles’ tent against Nestor’s advice. Agamemnon offers to return her and swears that he has not had relations with her.

l: Troy, The Iliad, BOOK IX.
s: Troy has not yet been taken, and Agamemnon briefly proposes that the Achaeans abandon the attempt. He nevertheless promises further rewards to Achilles if the gods later allow him to sack the city.

l: Argos, The Iliad, BOOK IX.
s: Agamemnon proposes returning to Argos after claiming that the Achaeans will not take Troy. He promises that Achilles will be honored in Achaean Argos and made his son-in-law if Achilles accepts the settlement.

l: ships of the Achaeans, The Iliad, BOOK IX.
s: The Achaean fleet is threatened by the Trojans, who are camped beside it and intend to burn its ships. Its defense becomes the immediate reason for sending the embassy to Achilles.

l: Achaean council, The Iliad, BOOK IX.
s: Agamemnon summons the Achaeans to a council in secret because of the army’s desperate condition. Diomed rejects Agamemnon’s proposal to sail home, and Nestor directs the leaders toward a night watch and an embassy to Achilles.

l: the embassy to Achilles, The Iliad, BOOK IX.
s: The embassy consists of Phoenix, Ajax, Ulysses, and the heralds Odius and Eurybates. It reaches Achilles’ tent, is welcomed and fed by Achilles and Patroclus, and presents Agamemnon’s appeal and proposed compensation.

l: Agamemnon's gifts, The Iliad, BOOK IX.
s: Agamemnon offers Achilles seven tripods, ten talents of gold, twenty cauldrons, twelve prize-winning horses, seven workwomen, Briseis, twenty Trojan women, a chosen daughter in marriage, a large dowry, and seven cities. He presents these gifts as atonement for taking Briseis and promises additional spoils if Troy is sacked.

l: Achilles’ anger, The Iliad, BOOK IX.
s: Achilles’ anger began when Agamemnon took Briseis from his tent and dishonored him. Agamemnon asks him to set the anger aside, but the unit ends while Achilles is still only listening to the embassy’s appeal.

l: the threatened destruction of the Achaean fleet, The Iliad, BOOK IX.
s: The Trojans have lit watchfires beside the ships and threaten to attack them at daybreak. Hector vows to cut apart their sterns and burn their hulls, and Ulysses warns Achilles that the Achaeans may perish unless he intervenes.

l: The Iliad, The Iliad, Achilles answered, “Ulysses, noble son of Laertes, I should give
s: Achilles rejects Agamemnon son of Atreus’s gifts and refuses to fight for the Danaans, declaring that Agamemnon insulted him by taking the woman awarded to him. Ulysses, Phoenix, and Ajax son of Telamon try to persuade him, but Achilles remains unmoved and plans to prepare his ships and return to Phthia. Phoenix recounts his own history and tells the story of Meleager to urge Achilles to save the Achaean ships before the danger becomes desperate. The envoys report Achilles’ refusal to Agamemnon, and Diomed advises the Achaeans to rest and resume the fighting without him.
